implementation_notes: The .NET platform supplies both halves. ConditionalWeakTable<TKey,TValue> attaches an arbitrary state object to any reference-type instance without modifying the type - it is documented as enabling compilers to 'dynamically attach object fields to managed objects', keys are compared by Object.ReferenceEquals, and an entry disappears as soon as nothing else references the key, so the attached attribute shares the subject's lifetime. The behaviour half is an extension member: a static method with the this modifier before C# 14, or an extension block (methods, properties, operators) in C# 14 and later, which makes the tuple (subject, attached state) usable as if it were a member. This is the route for classes you cannot derive from (third-party, sealed) and for per-instance attributes.
pitfalls: ConditionalWeakTable compares keys by reference equality, so a boxed value, an interned string or any equal-but-distinct instance gets its own entry, and value types (structs) cannot be keys at all - which is also why the table cannot attach state to structs.

The table does not enumerate its keys, so there is no bulk cleanup and no way to ask which objects currently carry the attribute; the value must not strongly reference its key or the entry is kept alive through the table (the classic dependent-handle leak).

Extension members bind only when the namespace is imported and always lose to a real member with the same signature: if the extended class later adds that member, call sites silently switch to it instead of failing to compile.

variants.name: WCF extensible-object contract (IExtensibleObject<T> / IExtension<T>)
variants.implementation_notes: When the subject is yours, the framework's own realization is a small contract rather than a side table: the subject implements IExtensibleObject<T>, extensions implement IExtension<T> and receive Attach(owner)/Detach(owner) callbacks, and IExtensionCollection<T>.Find<TExtension>() returns the most recently added extension of a requested type - Gamma's dictionary variation with lifetime notifications built in. Microsoft's documentation calls this the extensible object pattern and uses it to attach shared state or behaviour to WCF runtime objects such as InstanceContext, OperationContext, ServiceHostBase and IContextChannel, so extensions installed at different pipeline stages find each other through the subject instead of through ambient state.
pitfalls: Attach runs before the extension enters the collection and Detach after it has left, so an extension that publishes itself or reads its peer extensions during Attach can observe itself as absent - the documentation states the synchronization assumption rather than enforcing it.

Find<TExtension>() returns the most recently added extension of that type, so registering a second extension of the same type silently shadows the first for Find-based lookups while both remain in the collection and in enumeration.

The contract requires the subject to implement IExtensibleObject<T> and the extension to declare its owner type at compile time, so it cannot attach anything to a class you do not own - that is the ConditionalWeakTable route's job.
